newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers hold fast ahead of new talks.
newsitem.headline: French truckers hold fast ahead of new talks.

text.p: French unions urged truckers to continue a six-day-old blockade of about 30 towns on Saturday as employers agreed to a new round of talks in a marathon attempt to lift the pressure on the national economy.
Haulage bosses and unions were due to meet at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT in Paris after a second night session adjourned after six hours at 1 a.m. (0000 GMT) with little progress.

The companies have signalled readiness to yield on a demand that truckers be allowed to retire at 55 instead of 60. But unions say the talks are stuck over the issues of working hours and payment for all working hours, including time spent loading.
"The bosses still haven't realised the dangers inherent in the situation which they have generated," the Force Ouvrirere union said in a statement.

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago which badly dented his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe has called on both sides to end the dispute quickly and agreed that a Transport Ministry official chair the talks.

North of the south-western city of Bordeaux, where Juppe is mayor and singled out for the worst protests, truckers lifted a blockade on the A10 motorway overnight after earlier letting dozens of exhausted Spanish, Portuguese, German and British colleagues through.

But elsewhere there was no sign of a let-up. Since Friday evening, truckers have virtually blocked a motorway leading to Paris's wholesale food market in Rungis south of the capital. Police said produce was still getting through.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked motorways and a dozen fuel depots. The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and in Bordeaux.
Unions have said they would blockade Paris only as a last resort, adding that roadblocks 150 km (90 miles) around the capital would be more efficient.
Unions earlier accused employers of failing to negotiate seriously and said the next 48 hours would be crucial.

Thousands of foreign truck drivers, mostly British and Spanish forced to drive through France between northern and southern Europe, were stranded in the roadblocks, sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

The London Foreign Office ordered consulates in France to help stranded British drivers with money and contacts with home. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with French police in order to be able to claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
More than 1,000 British lorry drivers were stuck in blockades across France and British freight operators said the dispute was ruining them.
"We areand nothing seems to be happening despite our urgent pleas to UK, French and European authorities," said the Freight Transport Association.
In France, the Association of Food Industry said the protest was starting to have serious consequences on the industry's logistics and called for a rapid settlement.

The opposition Socialists sided with the truckers, who say they are underpaid and overworked due to cut-throat competition between companies. It said their demands for wage hikes, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 were justified.
